Thoroughly means doing something in a complete, careful, and exhaustive way — going all the way through every part of something, leaving nothing out, skipping nothing, and cutting no corners.

If you do something thoroughly, you don't stop halfway. You don't rush. You don't ignore the difficult parts. You cover every single aspect of it, with attention and care, until nothing is left undone.

1. Describing how an action is done

This is the most common use. Here, thoroughly tells you that an action was performed completely and carefully — every part of it, not just the easy or visible parts.

"Wash your hands thoroughly before eating."

This means: wash every part — back of the hands, between the fingers, under the nails — not just a quick rinse.

"The police thoroughly investigated the crime scene."

They didn't just glance around. They checked every corner, every clue, every detail — nothing was left unexamined.

"She thoroughly read the contract before signing."

She read every clause, every footnote, every word — not just skimmed the headlines.

"Mix the flour and butter thoroughly."

Don't just stir a little. Mix until there are absolutely no lumps left anywhere.

"The doctor thoroughly examined the patient."

She checked everything: blood pressure, reflexes, lungs, eyes — not just the obvious symptoms.

Notice the pattern: in every example, thoroughly tells you that the action reached all parts of the thing — not some, not most, but all.

2. Intensifying a feeling or state (meaning "completely" or "utterly")

Here, thoroughly acts like a powerful amplifier. It doesn't describe a process — it strengthens an emotion, attitude, or condition, pushing it to its maximum degree.

"I am thoroughly confused."

Not just a little confused — completely confused, confused in every possible way.

"She was thoroughly exhausted."

Not just tired — drained to the bone, every drop of energy gone.

"He thoroughly enjoyed the concert."

He didn't just like it — he loved every moment of it, completely and deeply.

"I thoroughly disagree with you."

Not partially — completely, without any reservation.

"She was thoroughly disappointed."

The disappointment was total. Nothing softened it.

"He thoroughly deserved the award."

In every way you can think of, the award was justified for him.

Here, thoroughly is not about carefulness or detail — it's about totality. Something is 100% that way, with no room for doubt or exception.
What Makes Thoroughly Different from Similar Words

This is where many learners get confused, so let's be precise.

Carefully — means you paid attention and were cautious. But it doesn't mean you covered everything. You can carefully look at one part of something and still miss the rest.

Completely — means 100% done, nothing left. But it says nothing about how you did it. You could have done something completely but sloppily.

Fully — similar to completely. Focuses on wholeness. But again, says nothing about carefulness or detail.

Thoroughly — combines both worlds. It means: you covered everything (like completely), and you did it with care and attention to detail (like carefully). It's the strongest word when you want to say both "all of it" and "done right."

Here's a contrast:

  • "He completely read the book." → He finished it. (Nothing more said about how.)
  • "He thoroughly read the book." → He read every part of it, paying careful attention to everything. (Both complete and attentive.)

A good way to remember thoroughly is to picture someone going all the way through something — through every room, every page, every corner, every layer — not stopping until they've seen and done all of it. The word carries the idea of being total and leaving no gaps.

Think of a detective searching a room. A thorough detective doesn't just look at the obvious places. They look under the furniture, behind the walls, inside every drawer — until every possibility has been checked.

Thoroughly is a strong word. It doesn't suggest partial effort or moderate results. When you use it, you're communicating maximum completeness. It's not like somewhat or fairly — it leans toward the extreme end of completeness and care.

Here are the words you'll most often see used with thoroughly, because they sound natural together:

With action verbs (process):

  • thoroughly clean / wash / rinse
  • thoroughly investigate / examine / research / review / analyze
  • thoroughly read / study / understand
  • thoroughly prepare / plan
  • thoroughly test / check / inspect
  • thoroughly explain / discuss / cover

With feeling/state words (intensity):

  • thoroughly enjoy / loved / appreciated
  • thoroughly confused / lost / baffled
  • thoroughly exhausted / drained / worn out
  • thoroughly disgusted / unimpressed / bored
  • thoroughly impressed / satisfied / pleased
  • thoroughly convinced / persuaded
  • thoroughly agree / disagree
A Few More Examples in Context

"Before the surgery, the hospital thoroughly sterilized all the equipment."

Every instrument, every surface — nothing was left with any risk of contamination.

"I thoroughly enjoyed reading that novel — every chapter kept me hooked."

The enjoyment was complete. Not a single part was boring or disappointing.

"She thoroughly prepared for the job interview — researched the company, practiced every possible question, and planned what to wear."

She left nothing to chance. Every possible aspect of preparation was covered.

"The app was thoroughly tested before launch, so there were almost no bugs."

Every feature, every device, every possible user action was tested.

"I'm thoroughly convinced that this is the right decision."

There's no doubt left in my mind. I'm 100% certain.
The Single Most Important Thing to Remember

Thoroughly = complete + careful + leaving nothing out.

Whether it's describing how you did something (you did all of it, with care) or how much you feel something (completely, fully, with no exceptions) — the core idea is always the same: nothing is missing, nothing is halfway done, nothing is left behind.
